512.title: Parashurama's challenge
512.hook: the wedding party is riding home when the sky goes dark and a man with an axe steps onto the road
512.carry: string this one, then we fight
512.howItsDone: Hindu tradition counts Parashurama among Vishnu's ten avatars, usually listed sixth, and his birth is marked on Parashurama Jayanti in the spring month of Vaishakha.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four couples circled one fire, and Janaka gave Sita to Rama as his companion in dharma. Your line was a companion on the way.

It should be a caravan of pure joy. King Dasharatha, his four sons, four new daughters-in-law, priests, soldiers and wagons of gifts from King Janaka, all rolling back toward Ayodhya. Then the birds begin to cry harshly. At the same moment, deer pass by on the right, a good sign. The king is worried, and Vasishtha reads the signs for him: something frightening is coming, and it will pass. A wind rises. The ground shakes. Dust hides the sun. And out of the dark walks a man with an axe on his shoulder.
screen: `A CARAVAN OF PURE JOY.` → `BAD BIRDS, GOOD DEER.` → `A MAN WITH AN AXE.`

segments.voice: Valmiki describes him like a fire no one can look at straight: matted hair, a bow in one hand, an arrow in the other, the axe across his shoulder. He's the son of the sage Jamadagni, from the family of Bhrigu. Later tradition calls him Parashurama, Rama with the axe, and counts him among the avatars of Vishnu. He's a brahmin, a priest's son, who took up weapons. After his father was killed in a feud with a royal house, the stories say, he made war on the warrior class again and again. Now he has heard that a young prince named Rama broke Shiva's great bow. So he's brought a bow of his own, and a story. Long ago, he says, the divine craftsman made two great bows, one for Shiva and one for Vishnu. The gods wanted to know which was stronger, and a contest broke out. In his telling, one great roar from Vishnu left Shiva's bow slack, and the gods of the story judged Vishnu the stronger. Shiva's bow passed to the kings of Videha; that's the one Rama broke. Vishnu's bow came down through Parashurama's own family, and here it is. String this one, he tells Rama, fit an arrow to it, and then we fight. Dasharatha begs. You're a brahmin. You laid down your weapons. You gave the earth away. Spare my son. Parashurama doesn't even answer the king. He speaks only to Rama. One Rama is facing another, and in later tradition, both are Vishnu come down to earth.
screen: `A FIRE NO ONE CAN LOOK AT.` · `THE SON OF JAMADAGNI.` · `TWO BOWS: SHIVA'S AND VISHNU'S.` · `STRING THIS ONE, THEN WE FIGHT.` · then, large: `ONE RAMA FACES ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Think of a challenge that came at you lately, from someone older, louder or very sure of themselves, and don't answer it yet; just notice the jaw, the shoulders, the belly. On each breath out, let one of those places soften: not giving in, just making room to answer well.

513.title: Parashurama's challenge
513.hook: Rama strings the bow, and then has to decide where the arrow goes
513.carry: leave me my power to move
513.howItsDone: In devotional readings this episode is heard as one avatar of Vishnu meeting the next, and the Bala Kanda as the happy prelude before the Ayodhya Kanda's exile.

segments.voice: Yesterday: an axe on his shoulder, Vishnu's bow in his hand, and a dare for a young prince. Your line was string this one, then we fight.

The king has begged and been ignored. The whole wedding party stands frozen on the road, the brides in their carriages, the soldiers with their hands near their swords. Every eye is on one young man, just married, who has been told to string a god's bow and then fight a warrior who has made kings tremble. You might expect a duel. Valmiki doesn't write one. What Rama does next is quick and quiet, and it ends with nobody hurt.
screen: `THE ROAD STANDS FROZEN.` → `A DUEL? NO.` → `QUICK, QUIET, NOBODY HURT.`

segments.voice: Rama speaks politely and firmly. He has heard what Parashurama did to avenge his father, he says, and he respects it. But you've taken me for someone weak. Watch. He takes the bow out of the sage's hands, strings it, and fits an arrow. Then the surprise. You're a brahmin, Rama says, and related to my teacher Vishvamitra, so I won't loose this at you. But a drawn arrow can't go to waste. It will destroy one of two things: your power to move freely through the world, or the worlds of merit you've won by your austerities. You choose. The gods, the text says, gather in the sky to watch. And the fire goes out of Parashurama. I gave the whole earth away to the sage Kashyapa, he says, and promised not to stay on it at night. Leave me my power to move. Take the worlds I've won. Rama looses the arrow, and those worlds are gone. Then the older warrior says he knows who stands before him: the undying Lord, the slayer of the demon Madhu. He walks around Rama with respect and leaves for the Mahendra mountain. Rama hands Vishnu's bow to Varuna, god of the waters, for keeping, and the family rides into Ayodhya to music and banners. Valmiki closes his first book gently. Bharata goes to visit his mother's family in the kingdom of Kekaya, and Shatrughna goes with him. Rama stays home, and he and Sita grow in love, the text says, each living in the other's heart. Remember that Bharata is far away. It matters very soon.
screen: `RAMA STRINGS THE BOW.` · `ONE ARROW, TWO CHOICES.` · `PARASHURAMA GIVES UP HIS WORLDS.` · `THE FIRST BOOK CLOSES AT HOME.` · then, large: `BHARATA IS FAR AWAY.`

segments.voice: Picture Rama on that road: the bow strung, the arrow ready, and a choice not to point it at the person in front of him. Breathe in and feel the strength you actually have; breathe out and feel how much of it you don't need to use.

514.title: the coronation planned
514.hook: the second book opens with an old king asking a hall full of people a question
514.howItsDone: Many Hindu families read the Ayodhya Kanda as the heart of the Ramayana, and Rama's habit of remembering kindness and forgetting wrongs is often quoted as a model of character.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama strung the bow and spared the sage, and the first book closed quietly at home. Your line was leave me my power to move.

Many people know how the second book of the Ramayana ends: a prince in clothes made of bark, walking into the forest with his wife and his brother. So notice how the Ayodhya Kanda begins. Not with a villain. Not with a quarrel. With an old man who loves his son, and a room full of people who love him too. For the next few weeks, almost everything turns on one family's household, and the first thing in it is good news.
screen: `BARK CLOTHES AND A FOREST: THE END.` → `THE BEGINNING: GOOD NEWS.` → `ONE FAMILY'S HOUSEHOLD.`

segments.voice: Dasharatha has ruled a long time, and he feels it. He loves all four of his sons, the text says, but Rama is the one the whole city talks about. Valmiki pauses to describe him, and one detail stands out. If someone does Rama a single kindness, he is pleased by it. If someone does him a hundred wrongs, he doesn't keep count. Generous memory is how Valmiki introduces the man about to lose everything. So the king makes a plan. He'll name Rama the yuvaraja, the young king, the heir who shares the rule while his father is still alive. He doesn't simply announce it. He calls an assembly: counselors, leading citizens, kings from the lands around. The text notes, a little pointedly, that in his hurry he didn't send for Janaka, Sita's father, or the king of Kekaya, Bharata's grandfather. I've carried this kingdom a long time, Dasharatha says. My body is tired. I want to put the weight on my eldest son. If you agree, tell me. If there's a better course, tell me that too. The hall answers with one roar of yes. And the old king tests them: why Rama, while I'm still ruling well? So they tell him. His truthfulness, his courage, his kindness to ordinary people, how he asks after their families and their fields when he comes back from a journey. The choice is public, and glad. That's why what happens next will hurt so much.
screen: `AN OLD KING, A LONG REIGN.` · `ONE KINDNESS KEPT, A HUNDRED WRONGS NOT.` · `THE KING ASKS THE ASSEMBLY.` · `WHY RAMA? THE PEOPLE ANSWER.` · then, large: `THE CHOICE IS PUBLIC, AND GLAD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one kindness someone did for you this year, small or large, and let it be vivid: the place, the face, what they said. If a hurt from the same person or the same year crowds in, let it sit further back for now, and spend the rest of the sit with the kindness.
Yuvaraja, the young king who shares the rule while his father still reigns. Dasharatha proposes Rama for the title, and asks his assembly, which answers with joy.
Your line: he doesn't keep count. One kindness kept, a hundred wrongs let go. See you tomorrow.

515.title: the coronation planned
515.hook: the king says tomorrow, and tells his son a hard truth about hearts
515.carry: the hurry is where the danger lives
515.howItsDone: Fasting and keeping vigil the night before a major rite is a common Hindu practice; in the text, Vasishtha instructs Rama and Sita to fast and sleep on kusha grass before the consecration.

segments.voice: Yesterday: an old king asked his assembly, and the hall roared yes. Your line was he doesn't keep count.

Some decisions are made slowly and then, all at once, rushed: the plan everyone agreed on for months, suddenly happening this weekend, because someone got nervous. That's where Dasharatha is today. The assembly has said yes. The obvious next step is to set a good day, send the invitations, call Bharata home. Instead, the king sends for Rama twice in one day, and the second time his voice is urgent.
screen: `SLOW DECISION, SUDDEN RUSH.` → `SENT FOR TWICE IN ONE DAY.`

segments.voice: First Rama comes to his father's hall, bows, and hears the news in public. Keep up your good habits, the king tells him, and rule gently. Rama goes home. Then the charioteer Sumantra comes back for him: the king wants you again. This time Dasharatha speaks privately, and he sounds afraid. I've had bad dreams. Meteors have fallen with a crash. The astrologers say my star is under pressure from harsh planets, and when signs like this come, a king can lose his life, or fall into trouble. So the coronation will be tomorrow. Then he says something honest, and a little chilling. Do it now, while Bharata is away from the city. Bharata is good, he says, devoted to his elder brother, self-controlled, kind. But the minds of people change, even the minds of good people. The king isn't accusing anyone. He's admitting he doesn't trust time. Rama goes to tell his mother, Kausalya, who has been praying for exactly this. The king has already told him what the night requires, and the priest Vasishtha comes to Rama's house to see it done: tonight you and Sita keep a fast, and sleep on the ground, on a bed of sacred grass. Rama and Sita bathe, make an offering, and spend the night quietly in a shrine. The love is real. The plan is good. And the hurry is where the danger lives. A king who once asked a whole assembly for its opinion now wants it finished before his own son can come home.

516.title: the coronation planned
516.hook: a whole city stays up all night getting ready for one morning
516.howItsDone: Abhisheka, the ritual bathing or pouring, is still part of Hindu worship: temple images are bathed with water, milk and other offerings, and the epic uses the same word for a royal consecration.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a fast kept through the night, and a coronation rushed to morning while Bharata was away. Your line was the hurry is where the danger lives.

The night before a big festival has its own sound. Pots clattering in kitchens past midnight. Ladders against walls. Someone sweeping a street that was already swept. Lights going up in trees. Children who should be asleep, absolutely not asleep. Valmiki gives us Ayodhya on that night, and he takes his time with it. He wants you to see how happy the city is, so you'll feel what it loses by morning.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE A FESTIVAL.` → `LIGHTS IN THE TREES.` → `SO YOU'LL FEEL THE LOSS.`

segments.voice: Start with Rama. Before the night's fast, he goes to his mother Kausalya's rooms, and Lakshmana is there. Rama turns to him and says, in effect: this is yours too. Rule the earth with me. You are my second self. A small line, and it tells you who these brothers are to each other. Then the city. Word has spread, and the people of Ayodhya can't keep still. Streets are sprinkled with water and strewn with flowers. Banners go up on the houses. Along the roads they set up lamps like trees of light, so night looks like day. People gather in the squares and talk of nothing else. The old king is going to make Rama heir, they say to each other. What good fortune for us. Meanwhile Vasishtha's helpers gather what the rite will need. The word for the rite is abhisheka, an anointing, a pouring: the heir is bathed with sacred waters. The text lists what's made ready: gold, white flowers, parched grain, honey and ghee, a white umbrella of state, yak-tail fans, a decorated elephant, waters from holy rivers. All for a pouring at dawn. And all of it, in a few hours, will sit unused. Nobody in today's passage is doing anything wrong. A father loves his son. A brother is invited to share. A city celebrates. Valmiki gives this happiness its full weight, so that when it breaks, nothing about it feels small. One person, though, has gone up on a rooftop, and she's looking down at all the lights.
screen: `YOU ARE MY SECOND SELF.` · `A CITY THAT CAN'T KEEP STILL.` · `ABHISHEKA: A POURING AT DAWN.` · `HAPPINESS GIVEN FULL WEIGHT.` · then, large: `SOMEONE ON A ROOFTOP.`

segments.voice: Picture Ayodhya that night, the swept streets, the flowers, the lamps in the trees, then bring to mind something good in your own life right now: a person, a season, a small routine you love. Let yourself enjoy it fully, without guarding it or wondering how long it lasts.

517.hook: a maid on a rooftop sees the lights, and the first person she tells is overjoyed

segments.voice: Yesterday: a city lit for a coronation, lamps in the trees, waters ready for the pouring. Your line was you are my second self.

Valmiki doesn't tell us much about where she came from. She's a maid from Queen Kaikeyi's family household, and she has always lived beside Kaikeyi. Her name is Manthara. The text says her back is bent. On the night before the coronation, she happens to climb up to a high terrace, the way anyone might go up to the roof to see what the noise is about. And below her, the whole city is glowing.

segments.voice: Manthara sees banners, flowers, people in their best clothes, music in the streets. What's going on, she asks a nurse nearby. Why is Kausalya, Rama's mother, handing out gifts? The nurse, delighted, tells her: tomorrow the king will make Rama his heir. Manthara goes down the stairs in a fury. She finds Kaikeyi lying on her bed. Get up, she says. Something terrible is happening to you, and you're lying there. The king is going to make Rama heir. Your good fortune is about to dry up like a river in summer. And here is the first surprise. Kaikeyi is glad. Truly glad. She sits up, delighted, and gives Manthara a beautiful jewel as a reward for the news. Then she says the line that matters most for everything that follows. Rama and Bharata are the same to me. I see no difference between them. If Rama is made king, what better news could you bring me? Before anyone whispers anything, Kaikeyi loves Rama. Quick retellings often make her the wicked stepmother from her first scene. Valmiki doesn't write her that way. He shows her generous first, so that when she changes, you see the change happen. That's why the story stays uncomfortable. The person who will send Rama away is not a stranger and not a monster. She's someone who loved him an hour ago. Manthara has heard all this. And she throws the jewel on the floor.
screen: `WHAT'S GOING ON DOWN THERE?` · `MANTHARA RUSHES TO KAIKEYI.` · `KAIKEYI IS GLAD, AND GIVES A JEWEL.` · `I SEE NO DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THEM.` · then, large: `SHE THROWS THE JEWEL DOWN.`

segments.voice: Think of a moment someone brought you news about another person, a promotion, an engagement, a win, and remember your very first reaction, before any second thoughts arrived. If it was gladness, rest in it for a few breaths; if second thoughts came later, just notice that they came after.
Manthara. Kaikeyi's maid, who sees the coronation lights from a rooftop and brings the news, and whose mistress is, at first, simply glad.
Your line: I see no difference between them. Kaikeyi's first answer is gladness. Until tomorrow.

518.title: Manthara
518.hook: how a whisper works: not one big lie, but a picture of the future
518.howItsDone: In Ramlila and in homes where the Ramcharitmanas is read, the goddess Sarasvati turns Manthara's mind at the gods' request; readers of Valmiki often note that his telling leaves the motive human.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Manthara on the rooftop, and Kaikeyi, glad, handing her a jewel. Your line was I see no difference between them.

A conversation like this happens in offices and families every day. Someone takes you aside. They're not angry at you; they're worried for you. Haven't you noticed, they say, how things are going to go? And they paint you a picture of next year, and in it you're smaller, and someone else is laughing. Nothing they've said is quite a lie. But by the end, people you loved an hour ago look different. That's what happens in Kaikeyi's room tonight.
screen: `TAKEN ASIDE.` → `A PICTURE OF NEXT YEAR.` → `NOTHING QUITE A LIE.`

segments.voice: Manthara throws away the jewel and starts building the picture. Once Rama is king, she says, his son will be king after him, and Bharata will be cut out of the line forever. Worse, a king fears his brothers: Rama will send Bharata away, or have him killed. And you, she tells Kaikeyi, were the king's favorite and looked down on Kausalya. Now Kausalya will be the queen mother, and you'll stand in her hall like a servant. Kaikeyi pushes back at first. Rama is the eldest, she says. He's good, he's truthful, he treats me like his own mother. After him, Bharata may well reign. Valmiki lets her argue; she doesn't fall at the first push. But Manthara keeps going, the picture gets sharper, and slowly Kaikeyi's face changes. By the end of the night she's asking: how? How do we stop this? Readers keep asking one question here: why did Manthara do it? Valmiki gives her loyalty to Kaikeyi and Bharata, and plenty of bitterness, and stops there. Later retellings add more. In some, including Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, the gods ask the goddess Sarasvati to turn Manthara's mind, so that Rama will go to the forest and, in time, defeat Ravana. That's a later answer, and a well-known one. Valmiki leaves the human version standing. And so the week closes: a sage's challenge on the road, a glad assembly, a city lit for a coronation, a maid on a rooftop, and now a whisper in a queen's ear.
screen: `MANTHARA PAINTS THE FUTURE.` · `KAIKEYI PUSHES BACK.` · `HOW DO WE STOP THIS?` · `WHY DID MANTHARA DO IT?` · then, large: `A WEEK FROM A ROAD TO A WHISPER.`
